title: Your First Agent: A Personal News Reader

scenes.narration: Welcome to Nabulines Academy. Today you're building your first real agent — a personal news reader that goes out, finds articles in your niche, and summarizes them for you. This is automation that actually saves you time every single day. By the end of this lesson you'll have a working agent running on your machine, and you'll understand every line of code that makes it work. Let's build it.

visual.title: Your First Agent: A Personal News Reader
visual.subtitle: Build automation that works for you every day

scenes.narration: What is an agent? It's code that runs on a schedule without you clicking anything. A news reader agent wakes up every morning, fetches articles from sources you choose, uses Claude to summarize them, and saves the result so you can read it over coffee. You're not manually checking ten sites — the agent does it for you. This lesson shows you the simplest version: fetch one source, summarize the top story, save it to a file. Once you understand this, you can expand it to any number of sources and any schedule you want.

visual.title: What This Agent Does
bullets: Runs on a schedule (cron) without you
Fetches articles from a news source
Uses Claude to summarize the top story
Saves the summary to a file you read
Foundation: expand to many sources, any niche

scenes.narration: Here's the flow. First, the agent fetches an RSS feed — RSS is a simple format that news sites publish so other programs can read their headlines. Second, it parses the feed to find the top article. Third, it sends the article text to Claude with a prompt asking for a summary. Fourth, Claude returns the summary and the agent writes it to a markdown file. Fifth, a cron job runs this script every morning at seven a.m. You wake up, open the file, and your news is ready. No browser tabs, no scrolling — just the summary you need.

visual.title: The Agent Flow
bullets: 1. Fetch RSS feed (news source)
2. Parse feed → find top article
3. Send article to Claude for summary
4. Claude returns summary
5. Write summary to file
6. Cron runs this every morning at 7am

scenes.narration: Let's build it. Create a new directory called news-agent and initialize a Node project. Type mkdir news-agent, then cd news-agent, then npm init dash y. This creates a package dot json file. Now install the dependencies. Type npm install rss dash parser axios at anthropic dash ai slash sdk. RSS dash parser reads RSS feeds, axios fetches web pages, and the Anthropic SDK talks to Claude. These three libraries do all the heavy lifting — you're just wiring them together.

visual.caption: Set up the project and install dependencies

scenes.narration: Create a file called agent dot js. At the top, import the three libraries. Require rss dash parser, require axios, and require the Anthropic SDK. Then load your API key from an environment variable — process dot env dot ANTHROPIC underscore API underscore KEY. If the key is missing, throw an error so you know immediately. This is the setup block — every agent starts by loading its tools and credentials.

Now write the main function. Call it async function main. Inside, define the feed URL — for this example we'll use Hacker News RSS, but you can use any RSS feed from any site you follow. The URL is https colon slash slash hnrss dot org slash frontpage. Then call parser dot parseURL and pass the feed URL. This returns a feed object with all the articles. Grab the first item — feed dot items bracket zero. That's the top story. Log it so you can see what you got. This block fetches and parses the feed — the first half of the agent.

Next, fetch the full article text. The RSS feed only gives you the headline and a snippet — you want the whole article so Claude has context. Use axios dot get with the story link. The response dot data is the HTML. For a real production agent you'd parse the HTML to extract just the article body, but for this demo we'll send the whole page to Claude and let it figure out what matters. In practice, libraries like Mozilla's Readability can clean HTML into plain article text, but that's an optimization for later. Right now we're proving the concept.

Now call Claude. Use anthropic dot messages dot create. Set model to claude dash sonnet dash 4 dot 6, max tokens to one thousand, and pass a messages array with one user message. The content is a prompt: you are a news summarizer, here is an article, give me a three sentence summary focusing on what matters. Then include the article HTML. Claude reads the HTML, ignores the navigation and ads, and extracts the article content automatically — that's why we can send raw HTML and still get a clean summary. The response comes back in response dot content bracket zero dot text. That's your summary.

Finally, save the summary to a file. Create a markdown string with the date, the article title, the link, and the summary. Use fs dot promises dot writeFile to write it to a file called today dash news dot md. Use utf dash 8 encoding. Log a success message. This is the output — the file you'll read every morning. The agent has done its job: fetched, summarized, and saved. At the bottom, call main dot catch to handle any errors and exit cleanly. Save the file.

Test it. First, set your API key in the environment. Type export ANTHROPIC underscore API underscore KEY equals your key. Then run node agent dot js. You'll see it fetch the feed, fetch the article, ask Claude for a summary, and save the file. It takes about five seconds. When it finishes, type cat today dash news dot md to see the output. There's your summary — a clean, three-sentence brief of the top story. The agent works. Now let's automate it.

scenes.narration: To run this every morning without you, use cron. Cron is a scheduler built into Linux and Mac — it runs commands at specific times. You write a cron job that says run this script every day at seven a.m. On Windows you use Task Scheduler, which does the same thing with a GUI. The concept is identical: the operating system wakes up your script on a schedule. You'll never manually run it again — the agent just works, every single day.

visual.title: Automate with Cron (or Task Scheduler)
bullets: Cron = scheduler built into Linux/Mac
Task Scheduler = Windows equivalent
Write a job: run this script at 7am daily
The OS runs it — you never touch it again
Agent works every day, zero manual effort

scenes.narration: Set up the cron job. Type crontab dash e to edit your cron table. This opens a text editor. Add a line at the bottom. Type zero seven asterisk asterisk asterisk, then the command. The command is cd into your project directory, then node agent dot js. The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. Zero seven asterisk asterisk asterisk means minute zero of hour seven, every day, every month, every day of the week — so seven a.m. daily. Save and close the editor. Cron is now watching. At seven a.m. tomorrow, your agent runs automatically.

visual.output:
# Add this line:
0 7 * * * cd /home/you/news-agent && node agent.js

# Explanation:
# 0 7 * * * = 7:00 AM every day
# cd /path && node agent.js = run the agent

crontab: installing new crontab
visual.caption: Schedule the agent to run at 7am daily

scenes.narration: On Windows, open Task Scheduler. Click Create Basic Task. Name it News Agent. Set the trigger to Daily at seven a.m. Set the action to Start a Program, and point it at node dot exe with the argument agent dot js and the start-in directory set to your project folder. Click Finish. Windows will now run your agent every morning, exactly like cron does on Mac or Linux. Same agent, same result, different scheduler.

visual.title: Windows: Task Scheduler
bullets: Open Task Scheduler → Create Basic Task
Name: News Agent
Trigger: Daily, 7:00 AM
Action: Start a Program → node.exe
Arguments: agent.js
Start in: your project directory
Done — Windows runs it every morning

scenes.narration: What you just built is the foundation of every agent. Fetch data from the web, process it with Claude, save the result, and schedule it to run automatically. You can expand this in any direction. Add more RSS feeds and summarize all of them in one report. Parse different sources — Reddit, Twitter, GitHub releases, anything with an API or RSS feed. Change the prompt to extract specific insights, like only security news or only posts about your tech stack. Add email delivery so the summary lands in your inbox. Or run it on a VPS so it works even when your laptop is off. Every agent you build from here follows this same pattern: fetch, process, save, schedule. You've learned the core loop.

visual.title: Expand This Agent
bullets: Add more RSS feeds → multi-source report
Parse Reddit, Twitter, GitHub, any API
Change prompt → filter for your exact niche
Add email delivery → summary in your inbox
Run on a VPS → works 24/7, laptop off
This pattern scales to any automation task

scenes.narration: One more thing: cost. This agent uses Claude Sonnet, which costs three dollars per million input tokens and fifteen dollars per million output tokens. An article is roughly two thousand tokens, and a summary is maybe one hundred tokens. So one run costs about one cent. Running daily for a month is thirty cents. If you summarize ten articles per day, that's three dollars a month. If you're on a Claude Pro plan at twenty dollars a month, this agent is essentially free because you're already paying for the usage. The point is: agents are cheap. The value they create — saving you an hour of reading every day — is worth far more than the few dollars they cost to run.

The time saved is worth far more than the cost

scenes.narration: Here's your exercise. Build an agent that summarizes today's top item in your niche. Pick a source you follow — a blog, a subreddit, a news site — find its RSS feed, and modify the agent to fetch from that feed instead of Hacker News. Change the prompt to focus on what you care about. Run it manually to test, then set up the cron job or Task Scheduler entry so it runs every morning. When you wake up tomorrow and the summary is waiting for you, you've crossed into the agent-builder tier. You're not just coding — you're automating your life.

You're moving from a daily summary to a real-time intelligence system. See you in the next one.
